title: Do Deterministic Verifiers Reduce Unsafe LLM‑Generated Network Changes? A Paired Shared‑Candidate Evaluation
abstract: We preregistered and executed a paired experiment (autocand_A1_prereg_v1) that measured whether coupling a deterministic NetOps verifier+gate (generate→validate→repair, max 1 automated repair) to a single LLM (gpt‑5‑mini) changes safety outcomes when the identical initial LLM candidate is observed with and without gating. Using shared_initial_candidate semantics, one sampled generation was reused for both arms per intent. We evaluated 200 deterministically selected paired intents in a sandboxed Batfish‑style validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5). All 200 shared initial candidates passed validation in both baseline and guarded arms (contingency n11=200, n10=0, n01=0, n00=0). The preregistered paired estimand (guarded minus baseline unsafe‑proposal rate) = 0.0; exact two‑sided p = 1.0; 95% paired‑bootstrap percentile CI = [0.0,0.0] (bootstrap_seed=1729, resamples=10000). No automated repairs were applied. Under shared_initial_candidate semantics the confirmatory contrast tests only validator/repair/gate effects on identical first‑pass candidates; it does not measure guarded‑conditioned regeneration, prompt engineering, or multi‑sample/model variance. We present the preregistered design, implementation and execution accounting, artifact‑grounded interpretation of the null result, and concrete recommendations for follow‑up designs that avoid ceiling effects.

sections.introduction:
Generative language models are being proposed to translate high‑level operator intent into device configurations and maintenance workflows. Practical deployment requires convincing evidence that model outputs do not introduce reachable safety or policy violations during change execution. Prior surveys and empirical reports emphasize that operational trustworthiness often depends more on surrounding system machinery—retrieval, deterministic validators, gates, and repair loops—than on the model alone [1],[2]. Architectures that combine generation with deterministic validation and bounded repair (generate→validate→repair) are widely advocated, but publicly reproducible paired evidence that isolates the verifier/gate effect on identical model candidates is limited [3],[4].

Research question. For an intent→configuration mapping task bank and a single LLM, does coupling a deterministic validator and deterministic accept/reject gate (with at most one automated repair attempt) to the identical sampled initial candidate reduce the incidence of unsafe proposals relative to observing that same candidate without gating? The study tests the specific estimand preregistered as paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline under shared_initial_candidate semantics (one shared initial sample per pair). Our contributions are: (1) a fully preregistered paired design and frozen execution (autocand_A1_prereg_v1); (2) an autonomous run with gpt‑5‑mini and a Batfish‑style deterministic validator on n=200 paired intents using shared_initial_candidate semantics; and (3) artifact‑grounded analysis, diagnostics, and recommendations for designs that avoid ceiling effects.
sections.related_work:
LLM applications in NetOps/AIOps include intent‑based configuration, runbook generation, RCA, and limited remediation. Several surveys and empirical studies document hallucination risks and the importance of deterministic checks and knowledge anchoring; these works commonly recommend validator‑coupled pipelines to mitigate unsafe outputs [1],[2],[5]. Generate–validate–repair and guarded agent designs have appeared in adjacent domains (program repair, robotics) and are proposed as practical defenses against hallucinated or unsafe outputs [3],[4]. Empirical DevOps/AIOps reports show retrieval and command‑safety checkers reduce unsafe command emissions in specific toolchains but stop short of offering universal guarantees [6].

Two methodological gaps motivate our design. First, prior evaluations often compare pipeline variants across nonpaired samples or mix regeneration semantics, making it difficult to attribute safety gains to validators vs. different model draws. Second, benchmark suites for LLM‑assisted NetOps lack tight coupling of intent tasks, deterministic validators (reachability/policy), and paired experimental protocols. Our preregistered paired experiment under shared_initial_candidate semantics directly addresses the first gap; it intentionally isolates validator/gate effects on the identical initial generation.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and frozen plan. The study was preregistered under autocand_A1_prereg_v1 (archived manifest). The preregistration fixed the estimand, sampling rule, generation semantics, model, validator, gating policy, repair budget, stopping rule, and analysis executor prior to observing outcomes. Implementation artifacts (task manifest, model configuration, raw results, and analysis outputs) were archived during the run.

Models, adapter, and validator. Model: gpt‑5‑mini (provider recorded as openai_responses). Orchestration adapter: hosted_netops_gvr_v1. Deterministic validator: deterministic_netops_validator_v5 (Batfish‑style checks of sequencing, reachability, protected interfaces, and field change preconditions). Task generator: deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5.

Critical generation semantics (explicit preregistered detail). Generation semantics = shared_initial_candidate: exactly one initial LLM generation was produced and deterministically reused for both baseline and guarded arms per paired intent; therefore the confirmatory estimand evaluates only validator/repair/gate effects on that same first‑pass candidate and does not measure any effect of guarded‑conditioned regeneration or sampling variance. This sentence restates the preregistered design choice and explains why a degenerate contingency is an interpretable outcome under the registered estimand.

Sampling and task bank. Planned task_count = 200 paired intents; selection was deterministic per the adapter index rule recorded in the preregistration. The task bank comprises synthetic intent→configuration items exercising workflow sequencing (VLAN migration, uplink failover, MTU upgrades), protected‑interface constraints, and minimum‑up group constraints. Each task payload encodes initial_state, required_sequence, allowed_touched_fields and difficulty metadata. The archived execution includes the full task_manifest.jsonl and per‑task reference answers.

Interventions and scoring. Baseline: observe the shared initial candidate produced by the LLM. Guarded: present the identical shared initial candidate to the deterministic validator; the deterministic gate applies an automated accept/reject policy and, if the validator reports violations, up to one automated repair attempt is allowed (maximum_repair_calls_per_task = 1). Primary outcome: binary unsafe_flag = any reachability or workflow/policy violation reported by the validator after candidate stabilization. Scoring rule used by the validator is the preregistered full_intent_constraint_validation; per‑episode validator traces (validation_before/validation_after) are archived.

Analysis plan (frozen). The confirmatory analysis used the registered paired_binary_analysis_v1 executor. Primary test: paired binary comparison (exact McNemar‑equivalent) on unsafe_flag between baseline and guarded with two‑sided alpha=0.05. Paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI computed with 10,000 resamples (bootstrap_seed=1729). Missingness policy: complete_pair_primary (pairs with technical failures are retried once per retry policy and excluded from primary analysis only if both attempts fail); the run produced no such failures.
sections.results:
Execution accounting. Planned_episode_count = 400 (200 pairs). Completed_episode_count = 400; failed_episode_count = 0; model_calls_used = 200 (one shared initial generation per pair). All per‑episode artifacts (responses, provider calls, validator traces, and scoring records) were recorded in execution/raw_results.jsonl, execution/provider_calls/*, execution/responses/*, and execution/scoring/*. Representative artifacts and a searchable execution_manifest are archived with the run.

Primary confirmatory outcome. The paired 2×2 contingency (guarded × baseline) was: n11 = 200, n10 = 0, n01 = 0, n00 = 0 (analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv). That is, every shared initial candidate was validated as safe in both arms. The paired estimate (guarded minus baseline unsafe‑proposal rate) = 0.0. Exact two‑sided test returned p = 1.0. Paired‑bootstrap percentile 95% CI = [0.0,0.0] (bootstrap_seed = 1729, resamples = 10,000). The analysis executor and resulting CSV artifacts are archived (analysis/results.json and analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv).

Repair and validator behavior. No automated repairs were applied in any guarded episode (repair_applied = false for all guarded episodes; repair prompt traces are null). Validator traces record parsed_command_count, required_command_count, observed_touched_field_count, and per‑interface final_state for each episode; representative examples (task‑000004..task‑000008) appear in execution/scoring/*. The scoring_reason_code for every completed episode was VALID_CONFIGURATION under the deterministic_netops_validator_v5 ruleset.

Latency and operational observations. Because the run used shared_initial_candidate semantics, the model was called exactly once per pair; model_call accounting shows hosted_model_call_event_count = 200. Guarded overhead was minimal in this run because no repairs triggered; archived timing logs (execution/execution_log.jsonl and analysis/analysis_log.jsonl) show median additional validation time per pair is dominated by deterministic validator evaluation rather than repair cycles. Exact latency distributions are available in the archived execution logs.
sections.discussion:
Artifact‑grounded interpretation of the null/degenerate result. Under the preregistered shared_initial_candidate semantics our confirmatory estimand isolated only validator/repair/gate effects on identical first‑pass candidates. Observing n11=200 (all candidates valid) is an interpretable scientific outcome: it implies that, for this model (gpt‑5‑mini), this synthetic task bank and prompt, and this validator ruleset, the initial sampled candidates already satisfied the validator constraints, so the guarded machinery applied no repairs and produced no different acceptance decisions.

Why the paired bootstrap CI is zero‑width. The paired bootstrap CI is degenerate because there are no discordant pairs to resample; every resample of paired outcomes yields the same paired difference (0.0), producing a zero empirical variance and thus a CI [0.0,0.0]. This is an expected statistical result under complete concordance and does not indicate a computation error in the analysis pipeline (the bootstrap parameters and seed are archived: bootstrap_seed=1729, resamples=10000).

Ceiling‑effect contributors and design implications. Plausible contributors to the ceiling effect include: (1) the synthetic deterministic task generator produced intents aligned to typical model capabilities for the chosen prompt/template; (2) the validator rule set mirrors the task constraints tightly so valid candidate outputs are probable; and (3) shared_initial_candidate semantics prevented the guarded arm from producing alternative guarded‑conditioned generations that might have differed in validity. To detect verifier value in future runs we recommend, in order of likely impact: (a) augment the task bank with adversarial or out‑of‑distribution items to raise baseline unsafe rates, (b) execute an alternative confirmatory design that uses independent generation per condition or multiple independent samples per condition (this changes the estimand and model_call accounting), (c) test multiple model variants and sampling temperatures to capture model variance, and (d) increase automated repair budget or allow iterative repair loops to evaluate repair effectiveness under nontrivial initial violation rates.

Reproducibility and artifacts. All per‑episode responses, provider traces, validator traces, task manifest, model configuration, and analysis artifacts are archived in the execution bundle (execution/raw_results.jsonl; execution/task_manifest.jsonl; execution/model_configuration.json; analysis/results.json; analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv). The preregistration id is autocand_A1_prereg_v1. These artifacts suffice to reproduce the confirmatory analysis within the same adapter framework and to rerun alternative analysis executors against the raw outcomes.

Threats to validity. Internal validity: the shared_initial_candidate design intentionally limits the inferential scope to validator/gate effects on identical generations; it is not sensitive to effects that require guarded‑conditioned regeneration. Construct validity: the binary unsafe_flag depends on validator coverage (sequencing, reachability, protected interfaces) and therefore does not capture risks outside those rule classes (vendor‑specific side effects). External validity: results are limited to single model (gpt‑5‑mini), single deterministic validator, synthetic tasks, and sandboxed validation (no live device execution). Conclusion validity: the run was powered to detect ~10 percentage‑point paired reductions under preregistered assumptions; the observed degenerate concordance precludes detecting any reduction because there were no baseline unsafe occurrences.
sections.conclusion:
We performed a fully preregistered, artifact‑grounded paired experiment (n=200 pairs) under shared_initial_candidate semantics comparing LLM‑alone observation to the same initial candidate after deterministic verification and bounded automated repair. Every sampled initial candidate satisfied the deterministic validator and the guarded pipeline applied no repairs; the paired difference = 0.0 (p = 1.0) with a paired‑bootstrap 95% CI = [0.0,0.0]. This null result is specific to the chosen model, synthetic task bank, deterministic selection, validator ruleset, and the shared_initial_candidate semantics; it does not contradict prior evidence that validators help under different experimental regimes (for example, independent guarded‑conditioned regeneration, adversarial inputs, or multiple model samples). We archive full artifacts and recommend follow‑up confirmatory designs that intentionally increase baseline unsafe rates or permit independent per‑condition generation in order to quantify verifier/gate contributions under more challenging conditions.

References

[1] N. Tu, S. Nam, and J. W.-K. Hong, "Intent‑Based Network Configuration Using Large Language Models," 2024. doi: 10.1002/nem.2313.

[2] F. Abu Zaid, D. Neider, and M. Yalçıner, "VeriFlow: Modeling Distributions for Neural Network Verification," AAAI Findings, vol. 40, 2026. doi: 10.1609/aaai.v40i33.40030.

[3] M. Bilal, J. Crowcroft, R. Wang, X. Xu, and S. Dustdar, "Large Language Models for Agentic NetOps and AIOps: Architectures, Evaluation, and Safety," arXiv:2605.12729, 2026. doi: 10.48550/arXiv.2605.12729.

[4] D. A. Alber et al., "Medical large language models are vulnerable to data‑poisoning attacks," Nature Medicine, 2025. doi: 10.1038/s41591-024-03445-1.

[5] S. Chakraborty, N. Chitta, and R. Sundaresan, "Automation of Network Configuration Generation using Large Language Models," in Proc. IEEE CNSM, 2024. doi: 10.23919/cnsm62983.2024.10814407.

[6] T. Cui et al., "LogEval: A Comprehensive Benchmark Suite for Large Language Models In Log Analysis," arXiv:2407.01896, 2024. doi: 10.48550/arXiv.2407.01896.

limitations: Internal validity: shared_initial_candidate semantics mean baseline and guarded conditions began from an identical initial candidate; the confirmatory estimand therefore measures only validator/repair/gate effects on that same candidate and cannot assess effects of guarded‑conditioned regeneration or prompt engineering.

Construct validity: tasks were synthetic and deterministically selected; the binary unsafe_flag depends on validator coverage (reachability and workflow sequencing rules) and may not capture all operational risks (transient performance regressions, vendor‑specific side effects outside validator rules).

External validity: single LLM (gpt‑5‑mini), single deterministic validator, and synthetic intents limit generalizability to other models, validators, production topologies, or live device interactions.

Conclusion validity: the observed null effect (paired difference = 0) reflects this execution's sampling frame where baseline generation produced only valid candidates; the study was powered to detect ~10 percentage‑point reductions but cannot rule out smaller effects under different sampling or adversarial inputs.
Operational relevance: no live device changes were executed (sandboxed validation only); operational benefits (reduced triage time, deployment safety) were not measured.
Security/contamination: adversarial or poisoning scenarios were not exercised; no retrieval‑augmented generation (RAG) was used, so retrieval‑based poisoning vectors were not evaluated.

Task‑bank reporting: the archived task_manifest.jsonl is authoritative for per‑label counts; manifest metadata indicates tasks are dominated by 'very_hard' items with a minority labeled 'extreme' (exact per‑label counts are available in the archived manifest).
